headline: Race Point at first light: bass to 34 pounds on live mackerel before the sun climbs high
subhead: The Bay's holding cooler water than the Sound and the Cape's south side, and that's buying us a longer window before the fish slide deep.
body_markdown:
Tuesday morning, 4:45, I had the boat idling off Race Point waiting for enough light to see the rip form up. There's a spot out there where the tide runs hard against the bar and you can watch it happen — the water goes from flat to nervous, then you get that seam, that dark line where the current stacks against itself. A guy I've fished with twenty years, Gary, was working the livewell, and he said what he always says this time of year: "They're either here or they're not." That morning they were here. First mackerel we dropped back into the seam got hit before it swam ten feet, and the rod bent over into the rail. Thirty-four pounds, fat, full of herring, came up thrashing in that gray early light. We had three more like that before eight o'clock, then it just stopped, like someone closed a door.

That's been the story on the Race all week — good, sometimes very good, but it's a window, not an all-day proposition anymore. We're deep into summer now, water's warmed enough that the big fish are doing what big fish do this time of year: feeding hard at first light and again toward dusk, then dropping down onto structure through the heat of the day. The difference for us up here is the Bay's still running cooler than the Sound or the south side of the Cape, so that window's staying open longer than it is for the boys fishing Buzzards Bay or the Vineyard side. We flagged this pattern last week and said it'd hold steady — it has. Race Point and Peaked Hill Bars are still giving up quality bass in the early hours, and that's not something everybody south of us can say right now.

Live mackerel on a fish-finder rig, 20 to 30 feet of leader, just enough weight to keep it down in the current without killing the swim — that's still the ticket on the rip. We're anchoring up-current of the seam and letting the mac drift back naturally into the disturbed water. If you're not catching your own bait, there are still pogies and mackerel schools showing on the sounder off the back side of Race Point, easy enough to jig up with a small diamond jig or Sabiki rig before you set up on the drift.

Peaked Hill Bars has been the secondary program — same tide-driven bite, same early morning window, but the fish there have run a little smaller, mostly schoolies up through low twenties, mixed in with a few bigger fish pushing thirty. That's typical for this stretch; the bars hold a lot of resident fish that don't move as much as the Race Point migrants. Bucktails, white and chartreuse, three-quarter to one ounce, worked slow along the bottom on the last of the ebb, have been picking at those fish when the mackerel bite goes quiet.

Cod fishing has been a grind, which is honest to say. Billingsgate and the deeper water off Wellfleet are holding fish, but you've got to work for them — jigging diamond jigs and teasers tight to bottom in 60 to 90 feet, and you might get two or three keepers in a morning if you're putting in the time and marking bait on the sounder first. The deeper structure out toward the middle of the Bay, where the whales have been working, is worth a look too — where there's whale activity there's usually sand eels and mackerel balled up underneath, and cod will sit under that bait column. It's not a fast bite. It's a patient man's game right now, and I'd rather tell you that straight than have you burn a tank of gas expecting a limit.

Bluefish have been scattered but present, mostly showing on the same rips as the bass, chopping up whatever bait gets pushed to the surface. Metal — Deadly Dicks, Hopkins — worked fast on the surface during that same dawn window has been drawing strikes, and a few of the blues have been decent, six and seven pounds, enough to make you check your leader.

Fluke's been a side dish, not the main course. Sandy Neck and the flats off Barnstable have some keepers mixed with a lot of shorts, and the better fish are sitting in that 20 to 30 foot depth where the water stays a touch cooler. Gulp on light bucktails, drifted slow, still the standard approach, but you're sorting through a lot of fish to find a keeper.

Tide's been the deciding factor everywhere out here — the rips only really turn on when there's enough current moving, so the two hours around the peak of the ebb or flood at Race Point and Peaked Hill are worth more than the rest of the day combined. Moon's past full now, tides easing back a bit heading into this weekend, which usually softens the rip bite slightly until we build back toward the next good push.

Looking ahead, if the weather holds calm like it has, I'd keep working that same dawn program at Race Point — anchor up on the rip before first light, live mackerel in the seam, and don't be afraid to leave once the sun gets up and the bite shuts off. Afternoons I'd rather be looking for cod on structure or working the Peaked Hill Bars bucktail program than sitting on a dead rip waiting for something to happen. The fish are here. You just have to fish the hours they're willing to work.
